summary: This is an interactive SSH host launcher that reads your SSH config files, parses them with Perl to extract host aliases and their descriptions, and presents a searchable list via fzf. When you select a host, it connects via SSH; you can also press keyboard shortcuts to perform actions like pinging or viewing raw configuration details.

explanations.8: If the target variable is empty, the function exits early — there's nothing to do without a target host.
explanations.12: This pipes three action options into fzf (a fuzzy finder), which displays them as a menu and returns whatever the user selects.
explanations.14: ssh -G retrieves the resolved SSH configuration for the target, and awk extracts just the hostname value so we can ping the actual IP instead of the alias.
explanations.24: read -k 1 -s waits for the user to press any single key without showing it on screen, pausing before returning to the list.
explanations.64: This concatenates all SSH config files together and pipes them into Perl to parse and format the data into a structured output.
explanations.65: The separator ' ;; ' is chosen as a delimiter to join multiple comment lines, so later we can split them back apart in the preview.
explanations.66: s/\r//g removes Windows-style carriage returns, and chomp removes the newline at the end of each line.
explanations.72: Each comment line is appended to a buffer, separated by ' ;; ' so multiple comments stay together but remain distinguishable.
explanations.78: When a Host line is found, we save its name and prepare to associate the accumulated comments with it.
explanations.79: Before processing the new host, we print the previous host's data so nothing is lost.
explanations.94: 150 spaces of padding ensures that the description text in the preview window doesn't get cut off when the main list is displayed.
explanations.98: The --query parameter pre-filters fzf results based on any argument passed to the sshf function.
explanations.100: The --delimiter tells fzf where to split the output line so it can use part of it (the description) in the preview.
explanations.111: The --expect option makes fzf return the pressed key (ctrl-a or ctrl-h) on the first line of output instead of executing the default action.
explanations.123: When fzf uses --expect, it returns multiple lines: the first is the key pressed, and the remaining lines are the selected data.
explanations.124: head -n1 extracts only the first line (the key), which will be empty if Enter was pressed instead of a shortcut.
explanations.126: awk '{print $1}' pulls just the first field, which is the SSH alias name we need to connect to.
explanations.128: If a key is non-empty, a shortcut was pressed, so we route to the actions handler; otherwise, proceed with normal SSH connection.
explanations.133: ssh -G outputs the resolved configuration for the selected host, including the real hostname, username, and key file to use.
explanations.140: ssh "$selected" connects using the alias, which automatically applies all settings from the SSH config.
